item.title: Fixing Matplotlib Subplot Overlap: Effective Spacing Techniques
item.description:
“Fixing Matplotlib Subplot Overlap: Effective Spacing Techniques”

Techniques for Adjusting Matplotlib Subplot Spacing

Here are several accepted and practical approaches to mitigate subplot overlap in Matplotlib figures:

Method 1: Utilizing tight_layout()

The matplotlib.pyplot.tight_layout() function or the figure method fig.tight_layout() automatically adjusts subplot parameters to give a tight layout. This is often the first and simplest solution to attempt.

Practical Implementation Example:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Creating a grid of 4x4 subplots
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=4, ncols=4, figsize=(8, 8))

# Apply tight_layout either to the figure or pyplot interface
fig.tight_layout() 
# Alternatively: plt.tight_layout()

plt.show()

This function dynamically calculates the necessary padding to fit all elements neatly within the figure boundary, preventing overlaps.

item.title: Python Matplotlib Scatter Marker Size: Decoding the 's' Parameter
item.description:
“Python Matplotlib Scatter Marker Size: Decoding the ’s’ Parameter”

When utilizing plt.scatter() in Python’s Matplotlib library, specifying marker dimensions through the s argument often leads to confusion regarding whether this value represents area, radius, or side length. How is the s parameter actually defined, and what mathematical relationship does it hold with the visible size of the plotted marker?

Defining the s Parameter in plt.scatter

The fundamental definition provided by the Matplotlib documentation states that the s argument represents the marker size in points squared ($\text{pt}^2$).
